title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The plain present plus a time word IS a future: naeil gayo is 'I am going tomorrow' and nothing more is needed. It is what Korean says for a settled plan, and it costs you nothing you have not already learned.

The fuller future is V-(eu)l geoyeyo, and it is not a modal. geo means 'thing' and -yeyo is the copula from M1, so gal geoyeyo says 'it is a thing that will be gone'. English 'will' is a word that sits in front of the verb; there is no Korean word doing that job, and looking for one is looking for something that does not exist.

The shape in front of geoyeyo follows the same kind of rule you already know: -l after a stem ending in a vowel (gada gives gal), -eul after a stem ending in a consonant (meokda gives meogeul). It is the third time this course has chosen an ending by the sound in front of it.
naeil takes NO marker, like oneul and eoje. There is no naeil-e. It can take the topic marker, naeil-eun, and then it sets tomorrow apart from other days.

an sits where it always sits, immediately in front of the verb — and with a verb built from a noun it still splits it: gongbu an hal geoyeyo. The future changes the verb's shape and nothing about where the negative goes.

Korean has other futures. One is used for offering to do something and one for guessing about the weather; neither is taught here. If you hear a future that does not look like this one, that is what it is, and it belongs to a later level.

sentences.cue: I will go to Korea tomorrow.

words.note: 'Tomorrow'. Like oneul, eoje and maeil it takes NO point-in-time marker. With the topic marker, naeil-eun, it sets tomorrow apart from the days around it.
'Korea', from M1, and here it is where you are going, so it takes -e.
The same marker M4 used for a point in time, now marking a destination: hanguk-e gayo, 'I go to Korea'. One ending, one job — putting something at a point — and the point can be an hour or a place.
'Go'. The stem is ga-, so the -yo form is just gayo — the stem's own a swallows the ending's, exactly as jayo does. gal is the shape it takes in front of geoyeyo, and it is the same verb.
The second half of the future: geo is 'thing', -yeyo is M1's copula. So gal geoyeyo is, piece by piece, 'it is a thing-that-will-be-gone' — why the future ends in the copula and has no 'will'.

sentences.trap: There is no word here meaning 'will'. The future is a noun phrase finished off with the copula you learned in M1, so the sentence ends the way haksaeng-ieyo ended — and a learner hunting for a helper verb will not find a seat for one.
sentences.sound: NAE-il HAN-goo-ge gal GUH-ye-yo. The k of hanguk softens into a g before the -e, so it runs as han-goo-ge. gal is one short syllable with an unreleased l, and geoyeyo has the eo vowel — 'guh', not 'go'.
